### Our material risks

Our material risks include insurance risk, where motor or home claims may be higher than expected, for example after storms; market risk, where investments, mainly bonds, may lose value if interest rates or credit spreads rise; counterparty risk, where a reinsurer or bank may not pay what it owes; and operational risk, including losses from failed processes, systems or people and cyber incidents.

Sustainability risks include physical risks from climate change, which can make storms and floods more frequent and severe, and transition risks, where investments may lose value as the economy moves to lower-carbon activity. Counterparty risk rose because more is now owed by reinsurers under the quota share.

We mitigate risk through motor quota-share reinsurance and catastrophe cover that limits losses from a single storm; underwriting limits and claims controls; and business continuity and cyber security controls. lt.P01: Turite teisę paprašyti šios dalies versijos oficialiąja tos ES valstybės narės, kurioje gyvenate, kalba, jei toje valstybėje narėje veikiame naudodamiesi įsisteigimo teise arba laisve teikti paslaugas. Lietuvoje taip ir darome. Norėdami paprašyti versijos, rašykite adresu sfcr-requests@brisendale-mutual.example.
lt.P02: Ši dalis anglų kalba pateikiama internete: https://www.brisendale-mutual.example/sfcr/policyholders/en
lt.P03: Brisendale Mutual yra savidraudos draudimo įmonė, priklausanti draudėjams nariams; ji neturi akcininkų. Esame įsikūrę Airijoje ir teikiame transporto priemonių bei būsto draudimo paslaugas. Taip pat parduodame būsto draudimą Lietuvoje gyvenantiems žmonėms, naudodamiesi laisve teikti paslaugas, bet neturėdami ten filialo.
lt.P04: Mūsų priežiūros institucija yra Home Supervisory Authority. Su ja galima susisiekti adresu enquiries@home-authority.example arba https://www.home-authority.example. Kadangi Brisendale Mutual yra savidraudos draudimo įmonė, ji neturi akcininkų, todėl niekas joje neturi reikalavimus atitinkančios akcijų ar balsavimo teisių dalies (didelės akcijų ar balsavimo teisių dalies). Brisendale Mutual nepriklauso jokiai grupei.
lt.P05: Nuo {{year_cur}} m. pradžios pagal naują transporto priemonių draudimo perdraudimo sutartį (kvotos dalies sutartį) perdraudikams perduodama nustatyta kiekvieno transporto priemonių draudimo poliso įmokų ir žalų dalis. Dėl to sumažėja mūsų prisiimama transporto priemonių draudimo rizika ir padidėja sumos, kurias mums skolingi perdraudikai. {{year_cur}} m. spalį kilusi audra sukėlė daug būsto draudimo žalų, daugiausia dėl stogų ir tvorų apgadinimo.
lt.P06: {{year_prev}} m. pradėjome parduoti būsto draudimą Lietuvoje, naudodamiesi laisve teikti paslaugas. {{year_cur}} m. tai nebuvo naujovė.
lt.P07: Pasirašytosios įmokos – tai mūsų parduotų draudimo polisų įmokos prieš perduodant bet kokią jų dalį perdraudikams. {{year_cur}} m. pasirašytosios įmokos padidėjo {{gwp_total_change_pct}}, nuo {{gwp_total_prev}} {{year_prev}} m. iki {{gwp_total_cur}} {{year_cur}} m. ## Part for policy holders and beneficiaries (dry run of the new format)
## A. Languages in which this part is available

You have the right to ask for a version of this part in the official language of the EU Member State where you live, if we operate in that Member State through the right of establishment or the freedom to provide services. We do so in Lithuania. To ask for a version, write to sfcr-requests@brisendale-mutual.example.
This part is available online in English: https://www.brisendale-mutual.example/sfcr/policyholders/en
## B. Business and Performance

Brisendale Mutual is a mutual insurance undertaking owned by its policyholder members; it has no shareholders. We are based in Ireland and provide motor and home insurance. We also sell home insurance to people living in Lithuania under the freedom to provide services, without a branch there.

Our supervisory authority is the Home Supervisory Authority. It can be contacted at enquiries@home-authority.example or https://www.home-authority.example. As a mutual, Brisendale Mutual has no shareholders, so no one holds a qualifying holding (a large holding of shares or voting rights) in it. Brisendale Mutual does not belong to a group.

From the start of {{year_cur}}, a new reinsurance contract for motor insurance (a quota share) passes a fixed share of the premiums and claims of every motor policy to reinsurers. This reduces the motor insurance risk we keep and increases the amounts that reinsurers owe us. In October {{year_cur}}, a windstorm caused many home insurance claims, mainly for roof and fence damage.
In {{year_prev}}, we began selling home insurance in Lithuania under the freedom to provide services. This was not a new development in {{year_cur}}.

Gross written premiums are the premiums for the policies we sold, before any share passed to reinsurers. Gross written premiums increased by {{gwp_total_change_pct}} in {{year_cur}}, from {{gwp_total_prev}} in {{year_prev}} to {{gwp_total_cur}}. Motor premiums were {{gwp_motor_cur}} in {{year_cur}} ({{year_prev}}: {{gwp_motor_prev}}), while home premiums were {{gwp_home_cur}} ({{year_prev}}: {{gwp_home_prev}}).

Net earned premiums are the premiums for the cover we provided during the year, after the share passed to reinsurers; net claims incurred are the cost of claims after the share paid by reinsurers. Net earned premiums were {{nep_cur}} in {{year_cur}}, compared with {{nep_prev}} in {{year_prev}}. Net claims incurred increased by {{claims_net_change_pct}}, from {{claims_net_prev}} in {{year_prev}} to {{claims_net_cur}} in {{year_cur}}. Net claims incurred rose because motor repair costs went up and the October windstorm caused many home insurance claims. Operating expenses increased by {{expenses_change_pct}}, from {{expenses_prev}} in {{year_prev}} to {{expenses_cur}} in {{year_cur}}; the reasons for this increase have not yet been analysed.

The net combined ratio compares claims and expenses with net earned premiums; the lower it is, the more of the premiums remains after claims and expenses. The underwriting result is net earned premiums minus net claims incurred and operating expenses. The net combined ratio rose by {{combined_ratio_change_pp}}, from {{combined_ratio_prev}} in {{year_prev}} to {{combined_ratio_cur}} in {{year_cur}}. Our underwriting result was {{uw_result_cur}} in {{year_cur}}, compared with {{uw_result_prev}} in {{year_prev}}. Investment income was {{invest_income_cur}} in {{year_cur}} ({{year_prev}}: {{invest_income_prev}}). Investment return rose by {{invest_return_change_pp}}, from {{invest_return_prev}} in {{year_prev}} to {{invest_return_cur}} in {{year_cur}}.
## C. Capital Management and Risk Profile
### What the capital requirements mean

> “Two capital requirements aim at measuring the financial soundness of the undertaking: the Solvency Capital Requirement (SCR) and the Minimum Capital Requirement (MCR). The SCR should deliver a level of capital that enables an undertaking to absorb significant unforeseen losses over a one-year time horizon and should give reasonable assurance to policy holders that payments will be made as they fall due. The MCR is intended to provide a minimum level of security to be held at all times by the undertaking and below which the amount of financial resources (own funds) should not fall.
>
> The capital requirements will need to be covered by capital (own funds) of sufficient quality to ensure that losses can be covered on a going-concern basis as well as in the event of winding-up”.
### Our capital position

At {{date_cur}}, our SCR was {{scr_cur}} and our MCR was {{mcr_cur}}. Eligible own funds to cover the SCR were {{eof_scr_cur}}, and eligible own funds to cover the MCR were {{eof_mcr_cur}}. The SCR coverage ratio was {{cov_scr_cur}} and the MCR coverage ratio was {{cov_mcr_cur}}.

At {{date_prev}}, the SCR was {{scr_prev}} and the MCR was {{mcr_prev}}. Eligible own funds to cover the SCR were {{eof_scr_prev}}, and eligible own funds to cover the MCR were {{eof_mcr_prev}}. The SCR coverage ratio was {{cov_scr_prev}} and the MCR coverage ratio was {{cov_mcr_prev}}. The SCR decreased by {{scr_change_pct}} between {{year_prev}} and {{year_cur}}, while eligible own funds to cover it increased by {{eof_scr_change_pct}}. The SCR coverage ratio increased by {{cov_scr_change_pp}} and the MCR coverage ratio increased by {{cov_mcr_change_pp}} over the same period. The new motor reinsurance contract reduced the insurance risk we keep (see Figure 1). Table 1 presents these figures.

| Minimum Capital Requirement (MCR) | {{mcr_cur}} | {{mcr_prev}} |
| Eligible own funds to cover the SCR | {{eof_scr_cur}} | {{eof_scr_prev}} |
| SCR coverage ratio | {{cov_scr_cur}} | {{cov_scr_prev}} |
| Eligible own funds to cover the MCR | {{eof_mcr_cur}} | {{eof_mcr_prev}} |
| MCR coverage ratio | {{cov_mcr_cur}} | {{cov_mcr_prev}} |
### Compliance with the capital requirements
Brisendale Mutual met its SCR and MCR throughout {{year_cur}} and at the time of disclosure.
### Our material risks

Our material risks include insurance risk, where motor or home claims may be higher than expected, including after storms; market risk, where investments, mainly bonds, may lose value if interest rates or credit spreads rise; counterparty risk, where a reinsurer or bank may not pay what it owes; and operational risk, including losses from failed processes, systems or people and cyber incidents.

Sustainability risks include physical risks from climate change, which may make storms and floods more frequent and severe, and transition risks, where investments may lose value as the economy moves to a low-carbon model. During {{year_cur}}, insurance risk fell because the new motor quota share passes part of the motor risk to reinsurers. Counterparty risk rose because more is now owed by reinsurers under the quota share.

We use the motor quota share and catastrophe cover to limit losses from a single storm. Our investment policy focuses mainly on high-quality bonds spread across many issuers, and excludes companies that earn most of their revenue from thermal coal. We also use underwriting limits, claims controls, business continuity measures and cyber security controls. Figure 1 shows the SCR by risk module.
![Figure 1: Solvency Capital Requirement by risk module, before diversification](chart_scr_modules.png)
*Figure 1: Solvency Capital Requirement by risk module, before diversification, at the end of {{year_cur}} and {{year_prev}} (EUR million).*
## D. Other information
Policyholders can send complaints to complaints@brisendale-mutual.example. They may also contact the supervisory authority.
Brisendale Mutual discloses the plans referred to in Article 19a of Directive 2013/34/EU. You can find them at https://www.brisendale-mutual.example/sustainability/plans

# Brisendale Mutual: Solvency and Financial Condition Report 2026

## Part for policy holders and beneficiaries (dry run of the new format)

## A. Languages in which this part is available

You have the right to ask for a version of this part in the official language of the EU Member State where you live, if we operate in that Member State through the right of establishment or the freedom to provide services. We do so in Lithuania. To ask for a version, write to sfcr-requests@brisendale-mutual.example.

This part is available online in English: https://www.brisendale-mutual.example/sfcr/policyholders/en

## B. Business and Performance

Brisendale Mutual is a mutual insurance undertaking owned by its policyholder members and has no shareholders. It is authorised and supervised in Ireland by the Home Supervisory Authority (fictitious placeholder). The authority can be contacted at enquiries@home-authority.example or https://www.home-authority.example.

There are no qualifying holdings because Brisendale Mutual has no shareholders, so no one holds a qualifying holding. Brisendale Mutual does not belong to a group.

We sell motor and home insurance in Ireland. We also sell home insurance to people living in Lithuania under the freedom to provide services; we have no branch there.

During 2026, we introduced a new quota-share reinsurance contract for motor insurance. A windstorm in October 2026 caused many home insurance claims, mainly for roof and fence damage. These events affected our risk profile: the reinsurance contract transfers part of the motor risk to reinsurers, while the windstorm generated a large number of home claims.

In 2025, we began selling home insurance in Lithuania under the freedom to provide services.

Our gross written premiums increased by 4.5% to EUR 1,158.7 million during 2026, compared with EUR 1,108.9 million during 2025. Motor premiums were EUR 676.6 million during 2026 (2025: EUR 641.4 million), and home premiums were EUR 482.1 million during 2026 (2025: EUR 467.5 million). Net earned premiums were EUR 976.5 million during 2026, compared with EUR 1,012.2 million during 2025.

Net claims incurred increased by 4.1% to EUR 683.0 million during 2026 (2025: EUR 655.9 million). Operating expenses increased by 2.2% to EUR 271.3 million during 2026 (2025: EUR 265.5 million); the reasons for the increase have not yet been analysed. Our net combined ratio increased by 6.7 percentage points to 97.7% during 2026 (2025: 91.0%). The underwriting result was EUR 22.2 million during 2026, compared with EUR 90.8 million during 2025.

Investment income was EUR 86.0 million during 2026, compared with EUR 54.7 million during 2025. The investment return increased by 1.2 percentage points to 3.5% during 2026 (2025: 2.3%). The effect of excluding companies that earn most of their revenue from thermal coal on investment returns has not been measured.

## C. Capital Management and Risk Profile

### What the capital requirements mean

> “Two capital requirements aim at measuring the financial soundness of the undertaking: the Solvency Capital Requirement (SCR) and the Minimum Capital Requirement (MCR). The SCR should deliver a level of capital that enables an undertaking to absorb significant unforeseen losses over a one-year time horizon and should give reasonable assurance to policy holders that payments will be made as they fall due. The MCR is intended to provide a minimum level of security to be held at all times by the undertaking and below which the amount of financial resources (own funds) should not fall.
>
> The capital requirements will need to be covered by capital (own funds) of sufficient quality to ensure that losses can be covered on a going-concern basis as well as in the event of winding-up”.

### Our capital position

At 31 December 2026, our SCR was EUR 373.1 million, compared with EUR 382.7 million at 31 December 2025. The SCR decreased by 2.5%. Eligible own funds to cover the SCR increased by 5.4% to EUR 820.6 million at 31 December 2026, from EUR 778.9 million at 31 December 2025. The SCR coverage ratio increased by 16 percentage points to 220% at 31 December 2026, from 204% at 31 December 2025.

At 31 December 2026, our MCR was EUR 108.7 million, compared with EUR 118.6 million at 31 December 2025. Eligible own funds to cover the MCR were EUR 769.9 million at 31 December 2026, compared with EUR 723.9 million at 31 December 2025. The MCR coverage ratio increased by 98 percentage points to 708% at 31 December 2026, from 610% at 31 December 2025. Table 1 presents these figures.

The main reasons for changes in the SCR and eligible own funds are not known from the information available for this summary. The motor quota-share contract reduced the insurance risk we retain and increased amounts owed by reinsurers; these changes affected the risk profile.

*Table 1: Capital requirements, eligible own funds and coverage ratios*

|  | 31 December 2026 | 31 December 2025 |
|---|---:|---:|
| Solvency Capital Requirement (SCR) | EUR 373.1 million | EUR 382.7 million |
| Minimum Capital Requirement (MCR) | EUR 108.7 million | EUR 118.6 million |
| Eligible own funds to cover the SCR | EUR 820.6 million | EUR 778.9 million |
| SCR coverage ratio | 220% | 204% |
| Eligible own funds to cover the MCR | EUR 769.9 million | EUR 723.9 million |
| MCR coverage ratio | 708% | 610% |

### Compliance with the capital requirements

We met the SCR and MCR throughout 2026 and at the time of disclosure.

### Our material risks

Our material risks include insurance risk: claims from motor and home policies may be higher than expected, for example after storms. Market risk arises because the value of our investments, mainly bonds, can fall if interest rates or credit spreads rise. Counterparty risk is the risk that a reinsurer or bank does not pay what it owes. Operational risk includes losses from failed processes, systems or people, including cyber incidents.

Sustainability risks include physical risks from climate change, which can make storms and floods more frequent and severe, and transition risks, where investments may lose value as the economy moves to a low-carbon model. During 2026, insurance risk fell because the motor quota-share contract passes part of the motor risk to reinsurers. Counterparty risk rose because more is now owed by reinsurers under the quota share.

We use the motor quota share and catastrophe cover that limits losses from a single storm to reduce insurance risk. Our investment policy focuses mainly on high-quality bonds spread across many issuers and excludes thermal coal. We also use underwriting limits, claims controls, business continuity measures and cyber security controls. Figure 1 shows the SCR by risk module.

![Figure 1: Solvency Capital Requirement by risk module, before diversification](chart_scr_modules.png)

*Figure 1: Solvency Capital Requirement by risk module, before diversification, at the end of 2026 and 2025 (EUR million).*

## D. Other information

Policyholders can send complaints to complaints@brisendale-mutual.example. They may also contact the supervisory authority using the details given above.

Brisendale Mutual discloses the plans referred to in Article 19a of Directive 2013/34/EU. You can find them at https://www.brisendale-mutual.example/sustainability/plans
